sections.heading: Why Collections Matter in DSA
sections.content: Almost every DSA pattern is built on a few data structures: arrays, lists, hash maps, sets, stacks, queues and heaps. Kotlin gives you all of them through its standard library and a few Java classes. Picking the right one is often half of the solution.

sections.heading: Array Examples
Array Tips
items: Use IntArray / LongArray instead of Array<Int> to avoid boxing
Arrays have a fixed size; use a list when the size changes
Printing an array directly shows a reference; use arr.contentToString()
Compare arrays with contentEquals(), not ==
Array<Array<Int>> is slower than Array(r) { IntArray(c) }

sections.heading: Lists
sections.code:
val list = mutableListOf<Int>()
list.add(10)               // O(1) amortized
list.add(0, 5)             // O(n) - shifts everything
list.removeAt(list.lastIndex)  // O(1)
list.removeAt(0)           // O(n)
val x = list[2]            // O(1)
list.sort()                // O(n log n)
list.reverse()             // O(n), in place

val copy = list.toMutableList()   // new copy
val sub = list.subList(1, 3)      // view, not a copy

sections.heading: List Tips
items: listOf() is read-only, mutableListOf() allows changes
contains() and indexOf() are O(n); use a set for repeated checks
subList() shares memory with the original list
Use list.lastIndex instead of list.size - 1
Use list.getOrNull(i) to avoid IndexOutOfBounds

HashMap: Group by Key
HashMap: Common Operations
HashSet
sections.code:
val seen = HashSet<Int>()
seen.add(4)                  // returns false if already present
if (4 in seen) { }           // O(1) average
seen.remove(4)

val unique = listOf(1, 2, 2, 3).toSet()      // {1, 2, 3}
val common = setA intersect setB
val all = setA union setB
val diff = setA subtract setB

sections.heading: TreeMap & TreeSet (Sorted)
sections.code:
import java.util.TreeMap
import java.util.TreeSet

val tm = TreeMap<Int, String>()
tm[10] = "a"; tm[20] = "b"; tm[30] = "c"
tm.firstKey()          // 10
tm.lastKey()           // 30
tm.floorKey(25)        // 20  (largest <= 25)
tm.ceilingKey(25)      // 30  (smallest >= 25)
tm.lowerKey(20)        // 10  (largest < 20)
tm.higherKey(20)       // 30  (smallest > 20)

val ts = TreeSet<Int>(listOf(5, 1, 9))
ts.first()             // 1
ts.floor(6)            // 5

sections.heading: When to Use TreeMap / TreeSet
items: You need the closest smaller or larger value
You need keys always sorted
Interval problems and calendar booking
Sliding window with sorted contents
Every operation is O(log n), so do not use it when HashMap is enough

sections.heading: Stack with ArrayDeque
sections.code:
val stack = ArrayDeque<Int>()
stack.addLast(1)         // push
stack.addLast(2)
val top = stack.last()   // peek -> 2
val popped = stack.removeLast()   // pop -> 2
stack.isEmpty()

// Avoid java.util.Stack: it is slow and legacy

sections.heading: Queue with ArrayDeque
PriorityQueue (Heap)
sections.code:
import java.util.PriorityQueue

val minHeap = PriorityQueue<Int>()                        // smallest first
val maxHeap = PriorityQueue<Int>(compareByDescending { it })  // largest first

minHeap.add(5)           // O(log n)
minHeap.add(1)
minHeap.peek()           // 1, O(1)
minHeap.poll()           // removes and returns 1, O(log n)
minHeap.size

// Heap of pairs, ordered by the second value
val pq = PriorityQueue<Pair<Int, Int>>(compareBy { it.second })
pq.add(Pair(1, 50))
pq.add(Pair(2, 10))
pq.poll()                // (2, 10)

sections.heading: Heap Tips
items: Kotlin and Java PriorityQueue is a min-heap by default
For max-heap use compareByDescending { it } (do not use negative numbers unless needed)
peek() returns null when empty, so check isEmpty() or use peek()!!
remove(x) on a PriorityQueue is O(n), avoid it in loops
Subtracting values in a custom comparator can overflow; use compareValues or Integer.compare

sections.heading: Custom Sorting
sections.code:
val nums = mutableListOf(5, 2, 8)
nums.sort()                                // ascending
nums.sortDescending()
val sorted = nums.sortedDescending()       // new list

val people = listOf("bob" to 25, "amy" to 30, "cat" to 25)
people.sortedBy { it.second }              // by age
people.sortedWith(compareBy({ it.second }, { it.first }))  // age, then name

// Sort 2D array / intervals by start
val intervals = arrayOf(intArrayOf(5, 8), intArrayOf(1, 3))
intervals.sortBy { it[0] }
intervals.sortWith(compareBy({ it[0] }, { -it[1] }))

sections.heading: Useful Built-ins in Action
sections.code:
val nums = listOf(3, 1, 4, 1, 5)
nums.windowed(3)               // [[3,1,4], [1,4,1], [4,1,5]]
nums.zipWithNext()             // [(3,1), (1,4), (4,1), (1,5)]
nums.distinct()                // [3, 1, 4, 5]
nums.maxOrNull()               // 5
nums.indices.maxByOrNull { nums[it] }   // index of max -> 4
nums.sorted().binarySearch(4)  // index of 4 in sorted list

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
items: Using List.contains() inside a loop instead of a HashSet
Using removeAt(0) for queues instead of ArrayDeque
Using java.util.Stack instead of ArrayDeque
Comparing boxed Integers with === instead of ==
Forgetting that map[key] returns a nullable value
Modifying a collection while iterating over it
Using Array<Int> instead of IntArray in performance-critical code

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: IntArray for fixed data, MutableList for growing data
HashMap and HashSet give O(1) average lookups
ArrayDeque works as both stack and queue
PriorityQueue is a min-heap by default
TreeMap and TreeSet give sorted order and floor/ceiling queries
Choose the structure based on the operations you need most
